title: Araby
focus: a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion

teacherSummary.text: A boy on North Richmond Street, Dublin, is infatuated with his friend Mangan's sister. When she mentions the Araby bazaar, he promises to bring her a gift. His uncle comes home late and drunk, and the boy reaches the bazaar as it closes. Seeing a shop girl flirt idly, he feels himself 'a creature driven and derided by vanity.'

segments.activity: Five key words in context, with verified word histories.
segments.script: Today's words: impinge — to press against or strike upon; converged — came together from different directions; derided — mocked or ridiculed; garrulous — talking too much, especially about unimportant things; pitilessly — without pity or mercy. “impinge”: Origin: Latin impingō (“dash against”). “converged”: Origin of “converge”: Latin convergere.

words.definition: to press against or strike upon
words.sentence: Through one of the broken panes I heard the rain impinge upon the earth, the fine incessant needles of water playing in the sodden beds.
These noises converged in a single sensation of life for me: I imagined that I bore my chalice safely through a throng of foes.
Gazing up into the darkness I saw myself as a creature driven and derided by vanity; and my eyes burned with anguish and anger.

segments.activity: Independent annotation and a claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph (exemplar given).
segments.script: Annotate the story for epiphany, imagery (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this story suggest about a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Araby develops the idea of a boy's romantic quest ending in disillusion. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of imagery and point of view shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: The boy's quest ends in a painful realization of his own illusion. When the text says “I imagined that I bore my chalice safely through a throng of foes” (Araby, paragraph 5), it shows this directly. He imagines himself bearing a "chalice safely through a throng of foes," but at the bazaar he sees himself "as a creature driven and derided by vanity."
